lesson_title: The Plant That Is Drinking Our Rivers
hook_text: South Africa pays thousands of people to cut down trees. Not for timber. Because the trees are drinking the rivers dry.
clip_script: Balance in the bush is a seesaw. Good rains, more grass, more impala. More impala, more lion cubs a year later. More lions, fewer impala. Fewer impala, hungry lions, fewer cubs, impala recover. Up, down, up, down, nobody falls off. Limits on food, water, space and predators keep it from tipping. Nature knocks the seesaw with drought, flood, fire and disease, and the bush heals in months or years. Then there is the guest who will not leave. Black wattle and pine, brought from Australia and Europe, left their enemies behind. They march down our rivers and drink far more water than the fynbos they replaced. So since 1995 the Working for Water programme has paid thousands of people to chop them out, because that is cheaper than another dam. Water hyacinth does the same to Hartbeespoort: blankets the dam, blocks light, rots, strips oxygen, fish die. Alien means brought here. Invasive means spreading and harming. That is the knock that does not heal by itself.
visual_style: A seesaw with impala and lion icons rocking; then a river shrinking as a row of tree icons advances along its banks; a chainsaw icon and a water-level mark rising back.
pacing: Rhythmic seesaw, quick list of natural knocks, slow reveal on the thirsty trees, crisp definition to close.
